2.1 b.)

It has a gradual upward trend from Jan to Dec, then dips after Dec. The trend and dips tend to stay consistent instead of growing or shrinking over time. The highest months are the Summer months and December. The lowest are January through April. The swings do not grow with the series, this suggests that using logs can create a proportional line to show the true patterns.

2.2 a.)

The chosen ARIMA model differences the series by subtracting the previous year’s (same month) value from the current year’s value (same month). The three letters from the ETS model say that the error, trend, and seasonal components are additive, so they don’t scale with the level.

2.3 a.)

215

2.3 b.)

The ARIMA model is most accurate because it has the lowest value for both RMSE and MAE. The two metrics do agree. They are both the lowest out of the rest of the models.

2.4.)

ARIMA vs ETS:

DM statistic: -2.9062, p-value: 0.004042

ARIMA vs snaive:

DM statistic: -10.755, p-value: < 2.2e-16

Because both DM statistics are negative, ARIMA has higher forecast accuracy than both other models. Both p values are below 0.05, showing the results are statistically significant. I would use the ARIMA model if I was a part of the liquor store chain because it has the most accurate forecasts.

4.1 c.) 120 forecasts for each variable. The date of the first forecast is Jan 1990. The date of the last forecast is Dec 2019

4.2.) var1 forecasts better for 7 out of the 8 variables. The smaller model could forecast better because it’s using solely the most recent quarter of lagged data and has to estimate fewer parameters. Adding more quarters can add unnecessary noise and more parameters to predict.

4.3 b.) BVAR with lambda 0.3 barely did better than OLS VAR(4). The reason why it barely did better is because BVAR uses the same data as OLS, but it adds priors through shrinkage. The BVAR uses relatively weak shrinkage (0.3), so it’s close to OLS. VAR(1) outperformed BVAR on the majority of the variables. Making lambda 0.05 actually worsens the model on ⅞ variables. It wouldn’t be a fair estimate because it only performed well for one sample. It should be used on multiple different samples to see the true best model.

4.3 c.) I tested on infl and got 1.4529. However, the p-value is above 0.05 (0.1489), so the results are not statistically significant. My results reinforce my idea that we should apply the models on multiple variables/samples to solidify their performance.

5.1 c.) INDPRO is turned into growth rates. PAYEMS is turned into growth rates. CPIAUCSL is turned into changes in growth rates. FEDFUNDS is turned into its first difference. They differ because using growth rate wouldn’t work on a set of values that are already percentages.

5.2 a.) 29.45% of the variance is explained in the first three factors.

5.2 b.) I would describe what the first factor is capturing as employment and general manufacturing. I would describe what the second factor is capturing as prices of certain goods and services.

5.3) In forecasting, you are only able to use data that was available prior to the time you were forecasting for. If you use data after that, it isn’t forecasting at that point since you have the actual data you’re trying to forecast.

5.4.) Factors do improve the forecast. The RMSE and MAE are smaller for the factored model than the AR model. The percentage reduced is: 10.43%. The p-value is below 0.05 (0.000443) making the results statistically significant.

Reflection

The models were most successful with the following situations: the VAR(1) model for forecasting macroeconomic variables, the factor model for forecasting industrial production, and the ARIMA model for forecasting liquor sales. Shrinkage and factors help reduce noise in the data and create a more accurate forecast, but more complicated models are not always the most accurate/best option. I learned that simple models are best when data sets with a lot of variables that don’t contribute much information for predicting what you’re forecasting. I saw shrinkage utilized multiple times to optimize models (such as changing the lambda in BVAR). The takeaway from this assignment is that simple models can, at times, be the best model to use. You shouldn’t automatically assume a more complicated model will be best for forecasting.
